claims.text: Mechanical loading induces short-range chemical ordering in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The stress-induced ordering develops both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Stress-induced short-range order locally impedes dislocation motion.
The local impediment of dislocation motion promotes crack nucleation and brittle behavior.
The proposed initial alloy is homogeneous and single-phase, with uniform elemental distribution and no detectable intermetallic precipitates.
Dislocation mobility is expected to vary across the proposed high- and low-temperature test regimes.
Applied stress amplifies local compositional fluctuations inherent to the high-entropy matrix.
Amplified compositional fluctuations form short-range ordered regions.
Short-range ordered regions act as barriers to dislocation motion and concentrate stress locally.
These ordered regions reduce toughness without requiring coarse intermetallic precipitates or extensive grain-boundary segregation.
Relative to the homogeneous baseline, mechanical loading will increase detectable signatures of short-range ordering.
Increased short-range ordering will accompany a measurable reduction in toughness, such as lower fracture energy or crack-initiation threshold.
The proposed mechanism is most likely under high stresses associated with cyclic or high-rate loading.
At extreme temperatures, diffusion may rehomogenize the alloy and make the proposed mechanism less dominant.
At very low stresses, short-range ordering may not be triggered.
